keeps: Refrigerator: use within 4 days. Garlic and herbs in oil can grow the germ that causes botulism, so Oregon State Extension says to keep any homemade oil with garlic or herbs, fresh or dried, cold and use it within 4 days.
Olive oil firms up in the fridge: let it stand 10 minutes and shake.
scratch.scaling: Keep the 3-to-1 oil-to-vinegar ratio; scale everything else with it.
safety: Keep it refrigerated and use it within 4 days (Oregon State Extension).

scratch.name: Dry breadcrumbs
scratch.summary: Day-old bread dried in a low oven and ground: the plain crumbs for meatloaf and breading.

ingredients.prep: day-old is best; any bread or crusts work

equipment: food processor or blender (or a zip-top bag and rolling pin)
steps: Heat the oven to 300°F. Tear the bread into pieces and spread them on a baking sheet.
Bake 15 to 25 minutes, stirring once, until completely dry and crisp all the way through and only lightly golden.
Cool, then grind in a food processor or blender, or crush in a bag with a rolling pin. Sift out big pieces for fine crumbs.
Italian-style: stir in 1 teaspoon Italian seasoning and ¼ teaspoon garlic powder.

plan.thaw: Use straight from the freezer.

keeps: Pantry: airtight once completely cool. NDSU gives dried bread crumbs about 6 months; if yours aren’t bone-dry, freeze them instead.
Freezer: in a bag, use straight from the freezer.
scratch.scaling: 8 slices of sandwich bread make about 1⅓ cups. Dry them in a single layer; crowded crumbs steam instead of drying.
notes: Uses store or homemade bread; the planner counts the slices.

scratch.name: Panko-style crumbs
scratch.summary: Crustless white bread pulsed into coarse flakes and dried without browning, for a light, crisp coating.
equipment: food processor, or the large holes of a box grater
steps: Heat the oven to 300°F. Pulse the crustless bread in a food processor into coarse flakes (or grate it).
Spread them on a baking sheet and bake 8 to 12 minutes, stirring once, until dry but still pale.
Cool completely before storing.

plan.thaw: Use straight from the freezer.

keeps: Pantry: airtight once completely dry (NDSU gives dried bread crumbs about 6 months); freeze them if you’re not sure.
scratch.scaling: 8 slices make about 2 cups of flakes.
notes: Save the crusts for dry breadcrumbs.

scratch.name: Croutons
scratch.summary: Cubes of bread tossed with olive oil and seasoning, baked crisp.

ingredients.prep: or any day-old bread, in ¾-inch cubes

steps: Heat the oven to 375°F. Toss the bread cubes with the oil, seasoning, garlic powder and salt.
Spread them in one layer and bake 12 to 15 minutes, stirring once, until golden and crisp. They crisp more as they cool.

plan.thaw: Use from the freezer; crisp them a few minutes in the oven.

keeps: Pantry: airtight, about 1 week for the best crunch; the oil goes stale after that.
Freezer: in a bag; recrisp in a 350°F oven for a few minutes.
scratch.scaling: Scales evenly; use two baking sheets for a double batch so they toast instead of steam.

scratch.name: Pancake and waffle mix
scratch.summary: A jar of dry mix for quick pancakes or waffles: add an egg, milk and butter.
steps: Whisk everything together very well, so the baking powder is spread evenly. Store airtight, labeled with the date and the directions below.

Pancakes: whisk 1 cup mix with 1 egg, ¾ cup milk and 2 tablespoons melted butter or oil, just until no dry flour remains (a few lumps are fine). Cook ¼-cup scoops on a greased griddle over medium heat, flipping when bubbles pop on top.
Waffles: 1 cup mix, 1 egg, ¾ cup milk and 3 tablespoons melted butter, in a hot waffle iron.
Buttermilk pancakes: use buttermilk instead of milk and add ¼ teaspoon baking soda per cup of mix.
keeps: Pantry: airtight in a cool, dry place. Use it within about 3 months, because opened baking powder loses strength in 3 to 6 months (NDSU).
scratch.scaling: Each cup of flour takes 2 teaspoons baking powder and ½ teaspoon salt; scale by the cup.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
scratch.yield: About 5 cups of mix, enough for 5 batches of about eight 4-inch pancakes.

scratch.name: Granola
scratch.summary: Oats, nuts, honey and a little oil baked slow until golden, with raisins stirred in after.
equipment: rimmed baking sheet lined with parchment
steps: Heat the oven to 300°F. Stir the oats, nuts, cinnamon and salt in a large bowl.
Warm the honey and oil together until runny, stir in the vanilla, and pour it over the oats. Mix until everything is coated.
Spread it on the lined sheet and press it flat with a spatula.
Bake 35 to 40 minutes, turning the pan halfway, until golden. For clusters, don’t stir; for loose granola, stir every 15 minutes.
Cool completely on the pan (it crisps as it cools), then break it up and stir in the raisins.

plan.thaw: Use straight from the freezer.

keeps: Pantry: airtight, about 2 weeks for the best crunch.
Freezer: in a bag for longer.
scratch.scaling: Scales evenly; bake a double batch on two sheets, switching racks halfway.
safety: Honey is not for babies under 12 months old.

scratch.name: Applesauce
scratch.summary: Apples simmered soft and mashed, sweetened only if you like.

ingredients.prep: about 7 medium, a mix of sweet and tart

equipment: potato masher, food mill or blender
steps: Peel, core and slice the apples (or leave the peels on if you’ll press the sauce through a food mill).
Put them in the pot with the water and lemon juice, cover, and simmer, stirring now and then, until very soft, 15 to 20 minutes.
Mash for chunky sauce, or purée or press through a food mill for smooth. Stir in cinnamon and sugar to taste, if using.
Cool in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the refrigerator.

keeps: Refrigerator: about 5 to 7 days (NDSU’s figure for opened canned fruit, the closest entry it has).
Freezer: leave ½ inch of space in a wide-mouth pint container (1 inch in a quart) and freeze up to 8 to 12 months for best quality (NCHFP).
scratch.scaling: Plan on about 3 lb of apples per quart (NCHFP’s average). Tart apples make a tangier sauce; 1 to 2 lb of tart apples per 3 lb of sweet ones balances it.
safety: To can applesauce, follow NCHFP’s tested recipe; this one is for the refrigerator and freezer.

nutrition.why: The peels and cores are left behind, so the numbers are USDA’s for unsweetened applesauce (sugar, if you add it, isn’t counted).

scratch.yield: About 1 quart (4 cups) from 3 lb of apples.

scratch.name: Pumpkin purée from a pie pumpkin
scratch.summary: A small pie pumpkin roasted soft and puréed: the from-scratch start for pumpkin pie, bread and muffins.

ingredients.prep: a 4-lb pie (sugar) pumpkin, not a carving pumpkin

equipment: rimmed baking sheet lined with parchment
steps: Heat the oven to 400°F. Wash the pumpkin, set it on a damp towel so it can’t roll, and cut it in half from the stem down. Scrape out the seeds and strings (save the seeds to roast).
Brush the cut sides lightly with oil if you like and lay the halves cut side down on the lined baking sheet.
Roast 45 to 60 minutes, until a knife slides easily through the skin and the flesh is very soft.
Cool until you can handle it, then scoop the flesh away from the skin.
Purée in a food processor or blender until smooth.

For pie, it should be as thick as canned pumpkin. If it looks wet, set it in a strainer lined with cheesecloth or a coffee filter over a bowl in the refrigerator for 1 to 2 hours, or stir it in a wide pan over low heat until thick.
Cool in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the refrigerator and stir well; pour off any liquid that separates.

keeps: Refrigerator: 3 to 4 days, as for cooked leftovers (USDA).
Freezer: pack in rigid containers, leaving ½ inch of space at the top of a pint, and freeze up to 8 to 12 months for best quality (NCHFP). Freeze it in 1¾-cup portions, one can’s worth each.
scratch.scaling: One pumpkin per batch. Two pie pumpkins fit on one large baking sheet.
safety: Home canning of mashed or puréed pumpkin isn’t recommended (NCHFP); freeze it instead.
notes: Big carving pumpkins are stringy and watery. Look for pumpkins sold as pie or sugar pumpkins, 2 to 5 lb.
Butternut squash makes a smooth purée the same way and works in any pumpkin recipe.

nutrition.why: Roasted pumpkin without the skin and seeds is close to canned pumpkin, so the numbers are USDA’s for canned pumpkin.

scratch.yield: About 3 to 4 cups from one 4-lb pie pumpkin. One 15-oz can is about 1¾ cups.

scratch.name: Simple syrup
scratch.summary: Equal parts sugar and water, for lemonade and iced tea.
steps: Heat the sugar and water, stirring, just until the sugar dissolves and the syrup is clear. It doesn’t need to boil.
Cool and pour into a clean jar. For a richer syrup, use 2 parts sugar to 1 part water.
keeps: Refrigerator: covered, in a clean jar. We didn’t find a published storage time for it, so make small batches and throw it out if it turns cloudy or grows mold.
scratch.scaling: Scales evenly.

scratch.name: Taco seasoning
scratch.summary: The packet’s worth of chili powder, cumin, paprika, garlic, onion and oregano, without fillers.
steps: Stir everything together.
To use: brown 1 lb of meat, drain, then stir in the seasoning with ⅔ cup water and simmer until thick, about 5 minutes.
keeps: Pantry: airtight, away from heat and light, about 6 months (NDSU’s figure for herb and spice blends).
scratch.scaling: Scales evenly. Mix a big jar and use 3 tablespoons per pound of meat.
notes: Chili powder is itself a blend that varies by brand; adjust the cayenne to your family.
scratch.yield: About 3 tablespoons, the same job as one 1-oz packet: seasons 1 lb of meat.

scratch.name: Chili seasoning
scratch.summary: A blend for a pot of chili made with 2 lb of meat or beans.
steps: Stir everything together.
Add it with the tomatoes and simmer the chili at least 30 minutes so the spices mellow.
keeps: Pantry: airtight, away from heat and light, about 6 months (NDSU’s figure for herb and spice blends).
scratch.scaling: Scales evenly.
scratch.yield: About ⅓ cup: one pot of chili (2 lb of meat or 4 cans of beans).

scratch.name: Italian seasoning
scratch.summary: Dried oregano, basil, thyme and rosemary in one jar.
steps: Crush the rosemary between your fingers or in a mortar, then stir everything together.
keeps: Pantry: airtight, away from heat and light, about 6 months (NDSU’s figure for herb and spice blends).
scratch.scaling: Scales evenly. Dried herbs from your own garden work well here.

scratch.name: Powdered sugar
scratch.summary: Granulated sugar and a spoonful of cornstarch, ground fine in a blender.
steps: Blend the sugar and cornstarch on high 1 to 2 minutes, until fine as flour.
Let the dust settle a minute before you open the lid. Sift before using in frosting.
keeps: Pantry: airtight, like any sugar (NDSU gives sugars 18 to 24 months).
scratch.scaling: Store powdered sugar has 2 to 5% starch to keep it from caking (Wikipedia); a tablespoon per cup of sugar is about 4%. It comes out a little less fine than store powdered sugar.
notes: For whipped cream and dusting, granulated sugar ground alone works too.

scratch.name: Brown sugar
scratch.summary: White sugar with a little molasses worked in: light or dark.

ingredients.prep: for dark brown; use 1½ teaspoons for light

equipment: bowl and fork, or a mixer
steps: Work the molasses into the sugar with a fork (or a mixer on low) until the color is even and there are no streaks.
keeps: Pantry: airtight, or it dries out and hardens (NDSU gives sugars 18 to 24 months).
scratch.scaling: Store brown sugar is white sugar with molasses added: about 3.5% molasses for light and 6.5% for dark, by volume (Wikipedia). That is about 1½ teaspoons (light) or 1 tablespoon (dark) per cup. NDSU’s chart uses ¼ cup molasses per cup of sugar, which makes a much darker, wetter sugar.
notes: In a pinch, plain white sugar also works cup for cup (USU, Missouri), with less caramel flavor.

scratch.name: Self-rising flour
scratch.summary: All-purpose flour with the baking powder and salt already in it.
steps: Whisk the flour, baking powder and salt together very well.
keeps: Mix it as you need it: it lasts only as long as the baking powder, which loses strength 3 to 6 months after opening (NDSU).
scratch.scaling: Per cup: 1 cup minus 2 teaspoons all-purpose flour, 1½ teaspoons baking powder and ½ teaspoon salt (NDSU and University of Missouri; Colorado State uses 1¼ teaspoons baking powder and ¼ teaspoon salt).
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).

scratch.name: Cake flour
scratch.summary: Less all-purpose flour, sifted, for a tender cake.
steps: For each cup of cake flour, measure 1 cup minus 2 tablespoons of all-purpose flour and sift it.
keeps: Pantry: as for flour (NDSU: 6 to 8 months once opened).
scratch.scaling: 1 cup cake flour = 1 cup minus 2 tablespoons all-purpose (NDSU, Missouri, Colorado State).
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).

scratch.name: Buttermilk stand-in
scratch.summary: Milk soured with lemon juice or vinegar, for baking when you’re out of buttermilk.

ingredients.prep: enough to make 1 cup with the lemon

steps: Put the lemon juice in a measuring cup and add milk to the 1-cup line.
Stir and let it stand 5 to 10 minutes, until slightly thickened.
keeps: Use it right away, in the recipe.
scratch.scaling: 1 tablespoon lemon juice or vinegar per cup (NDSU, Missouri, Colorado State, USU). Plain yogurt also stands in cup for cup (Missouri).
notes: It works in pancakes, biscuits and cakes, where the acid reacts with baking soda. It’s thinner than cultured buttermilk.

scratch.name: Black beans from dry
scratch.summary: A pound of dried beans soaked and simmered: about as much as four cans, for a fraction of the cost.

ingredients.prep: about 10 cups to soak and 10 to cook

steps: Spread the beans on a tray and pick out any small stones or shriveled beans, then rinse them.
Soak them in plenty of cold water (about 10 cups) at least 5 hours or overnight.

Drain and rinse. Cover with fresh water by about 2 inches, add the bay leaf, and bring to a boil. Boil hard for at least 30 minutes: soaking and then boiling in fresh water for at least 30 minutes destroys a natural toxin in raw beans, especially kidney beans (FDA).
Turn the heat down and simmer, partly covered, until tender all the way through, 1 to 1½ hours in all depending on the age of the beans. Add the salt in the last 15 minutes.
Cool them in their liquid in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours. Freeze them in their liquid in can-sized portions (about 1½ cups each).

stages.do: Boil hard, then simmer until tender

plan.thaw: Thaw in the refrigerator, or warm them straight from frozen in a covered pot.

keeps: Refrigerator: 3 to 4 days, as for other cooked leftovers (USDA).
Freezer: 3 to 4 months in their liquid (USDA’s time for leftovers).
scratch.scaling: 1 lb of dried beans makes about 6 cups cooked, about four 15-oz cans. Use a pot big enough that the beans stay covered by 2 inches of water.
safety: Never eat raw or undercooked dried beans. Soak at least 5 hours and boil in fresh water at least 30 minutes (FDA).
Cool in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours (USDA).
scratch.yield: About 6 cups of cooked beans, drained: about the same as four 15-oz cans.

scratch.name: Pinto beans from dry
scratch.summary: A pound of dried beans soaked and simmered: about as much as four cans, for a fraction of the cost.

ingredients.prep: about 10 cups to soak and 10 to cook

steps: Spread the beans on a tray and pick out any small stones or shriveled beans, then rinse them.
Soak them in plenty of cold water (about 10 cups) at least 5 hours or overnight.

Drain and rinse. Cover with fresh water by about 2 inches, add the bay leaf, and bring to a boil. Boil hard for at least 30 minutes: soaking and then boiling in fresh water for at least 30 minutes destroys a natural toxin in raw beans, especially kidney beans (FDA).
Turn the heat down and simmer, partly covered, until tender all the way through, 1½ to 2 hours in all depending on the age of the beans. Add the salt in the last 15 minutes.
Cool them in their liquid in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours. Freeze them in their liquid in can-sized portions (about 1½ cups each).

scratch.name: Marshmallows
scratch.summary: Soft vanilla marshmallows from gelatin, sugar and syrup, whipped, set in a pan and cut into squares.
equipment: stand mixer with whisk (or a strong hand mixer)
steps: Oil the pan lightly. Sift the powdered sugar and cornstarch together; dust the pan with about 2 tablespoons of the mix.
Pour ½ cup of the cold water into the mixer bowl and sprinkle the gelatin over it. Let it soak (bloom) while you make the syrup.

In the saucepan, stir the sugar, corn syrup, salt and the other ½ cup water over medium heat until the sugar dissolves. Clip on the thermometer and boil without stirring to 240°F (115°C), the soft-ball stage, about 10 to 12 minutes.
Turn the mixer to low. Pour the hot syrup in a thin stream down the side of the bowl, away from the whisk, so it doesn’t spatter.
Turn the mixer to high and whip 10 to 12 minutes, until the mixture is thick, white, glossy and just warm, and holds a ribbon. Whip in the vanilla for the last minute.
Scrape it into the pan with the oiled spatula and smooth the top with an oiled hand or spatula. Dust the top.
Leave it uncovered at room temperature at least 4 hours, or overnight, to set.
Turn the slab out onto a board dusted with the sugar mix. Cut into 1½-inch squares with an oiled knife or pizza cutter, and toss the cut sides in the rest of the mix so they don’t stick.

stages.do: Bloom the gelatin and cook the syrup to 240°F

keeps: Pantry: airtight, dusted, at room temperature. NDSU gives opened marshmallows about 1 month; homemade ones are softest in the first week or two.
scratch.scaling: An 8 × 8-inch pan takes half a batch (and gives thicker squares); the syrup still cooks to 240°F, a little faster. Small batches are hard to read on a thermometer, so use a small, deep pan.
scratch.old_way: The name comes from the marsh mallow plant: its root sap was once whipped with sugar into a soft candy. Gelatin took the root’s place in the late 1800s, and that is the marshmallow we know.
safety: Hot sugar syrup is far hotter than boiling water and sticks to skin. Keep children back while it cooks and while you pour it, use a deep pan, and don’t taste it until it cools.
Test your candy thermometer first: in boiling water it should read 212°F at sea level. Above sea level, cook to 2°F less for every 1,000 feet (Colorado State University Extension).
notes: Golden syrup or light corn syrup both work; the syrup keeps the sugar from crystallizing.
Some recipes cook the syrup a little higher, to 245 or 250°F, for a firmer marshmallow.
For toasting, cut them bigger (2 inches) and let them dry, uncovered, a few extra hours; drier marshmallows hold their shape over a fire.

scratch.name: Chocolate from cocoa powder and cocoa butter
scratch.summary: The easy way: melt cocoa butter, whisk in cocoa powder and sugar, and pour it into bars. Reliable, about 30 minutes.

makes.label: g of dark chocolate (about two 4-oz bars)

equipment: heatproof bowl over a pan of barely simmering water (or a microwave)
chocolate mold, small loaf pan or parchment-lined dish
steps: Melt the cocoa butter in the bowl over barely simmering water, stirring, until it is clear and about 115 to 120°F. Keep every drop of water and steam out: a little water makes chocolate seize, turning it thick and grainy.
Take the bowl off the heat. Whisk in the sifted cocoa, powdered sugar and salt a spoonful at a time until it is completely smooth, 3 to 4 minutes. Add the vanilla if you like.
Stir now and then as it cools to about 90°F so the cocoa stays mixed in. For snap and shine, temper it now by the seed method in the note below; otherwise go on.
Pour it into the mold or lined pan and tap it on the counter to pop the bubbles.
Let it set at cool room temperature, about 1 hour, or 20 minutes in the refrigerator. Unmold and break into pieces.

stages.do: Whisk in the cocoa and sugar, and cool while stirring

keeps: Cool, dry place, wrapped, at 60 to 70°F, away from strong smells. NDSU gives opened chocolate about 1 year; homemade chocolate without emulsifiers can turn dull or streaky sooner, which is harmless.
scratch.scaling: Keep the weights in proportion: about 40 percent cocoa butter, 25 percent cocoa and 30 percent sugar. More sugar makes it sweeter and milder.
scratch.old_way: Solid eating chocolate is younger than you might think. In 1828 Coenraad van Houten patented a press that squeezed cocoa butter out of ground cocoa beans, leaving cocoa powder; putting extra cocoa butter back in is what made smooth bars possible.
notes: Tempering is what gives chocolate a snap and a shine. Seed method: melt dark chocolate to 120 to 122°F (milk chocolate to 115 to 117°F), then stir in chopped tempered chocolate, about a quarter of the weight, until it cools to 88 to 90°F for dark (86 to 88°F for milk). Fish out any unmelted pieces. Test a smear on foil: at room temperature it should set firm and glossy in about 5 minutes.
Untempered, this chocolate still tastes good: it sets soft and matte and melts at warm room temperature. For s’mores, which melt it anyway, that is fine.
Milk chocolate: use 100 g cocoa butter, 30 g cocoa, 40 g whole milk powder and 80 g powdered sugar, and temper to 86 to 88°F.
Granulated sugar stays gritty; powdered sugar (or sugar ground fine in a blender) melts in smoothly.
scratch.yield: About 8 oz (230 g) of dark chocolate, roughly 60 percent cocoa.

scratch.name: Bean-to-bar chocolate
scratch.summary: The hard way, for the curious: roast cocoa beans, crack and winnow them, grind and refine them with sugar, then temper. A project, not a weeknight.

ingredients.prep: roasted nibs, or about 375 g of whole cocoa beans to roast and shell
helps a home grinder; leave out for a stiffer bar

equipment: hair dryer or a fan, and two bowls (for winnowing)
stone melanger (best), or a high-powered blender or food processor
steps: Buy cocoa beans or nibs sold as food. If you start with whole beans, roast them in one layer at about 300°F for 20 to 30 minutes, until they smell like brownies and the shells crackle and loosen. Roasts vary by bean; taste a cooled bean and adjust next time.
Cool the beans, put them in the bag and crack them with the rolling pin into pieces the size of a lentil.

Winnow: outdoors or over a sink, pour the cracked beans slowly from one bowl to the other while a hair dryer on cool (or a fan) blows across the stream. The light papery shells blow away; the heavy nibs fall into the bowl. Repeat until the nibs are clean.

Grind: blend the nibs (and the cocoa butter, if using) in short bursts, scraping down often, until the friction warms them into a thick, gritty paste, cocoa liquor. Let the motor rest between bursts so it doesn’t overheat.

Refine: in a melanger, add the paste and sugar (and milk powder for milk chocolate) and let it run 24 to 72 hours, tasting now and then, until it feels smooth on your tongue. With only a blender, grind the sugar fine first, blend it in for 10 to 15 minutes, and expect a rustic, slightly gritty bar.

Temper by the seed method: warm the chocolate to 120°F, then stir in about a quarter of its weight of chopped tempered chocolate (from an earlier batch or a good store bar) until it cools to 88 to 90°F (86 to 88°F for milk). Test a smear on foil: it should set glossy and firm in about 5 minutes.
Pour into molds, tap out the bubbles, and let it set at cool room temperature, about 1 hour.

stages.do: Refine in a melanger (skip for a rustic bar)

keeps: Cool, dry place, wrapped, at 60 to 70°F, away from strong smells. NDSU gives opened chocolate about 1 year.
scratch.scaling: Melangers have a minimum load (often about 1 lb of nibs); a blender works best with 1 to 2 cups of nibs at a time. Keep the sugar at about a quarter of the weight for a 75 percent bar.
scratch.old_way: For most of its history chocolate was a drink: roasted beans ground on a warm stone and whisked with water and spices. Bars came only in the 1800s, once presses and refining machines could make the paste smooth.
safety: A blender jar and a melanger drum get hot as they run; handle them with care, and keep fingers out of a running machine.
notes: Tempering is what gives chocolate a snap and a shine. Seed method: melt dark chocolate to 120 to 122°F (milk chocolate to 115 to 117°F), then stir in chopped tempered chocolate, about a quarter of the weight, until it cools to 88 to 90°F for dark (86 to 88°F for milk). Fish out any unmelted pieces. Test a smear on foil: at room temperature it should set firm and glossy in about 5 minutes.

Realistic expectations: a blender can’t grind sugar and cocoa as fine as a factory, so the first bars are often grainy. A melanger, a small stone grinder made for nut butters and chocolate, is what makes home bars smooth.

No seed chocolate? Pour two-thirds of the melted chocolate onto a clean marble or granite slab, spread and scrape it back and forth until it thickens, then stir it back into the rest; this tabling method is how chocolatiers temper by hand.
scratch.yield: About 13 oz (380 g) of 75 percent dark chocolate.

scratch.name: Graham crackers
scratch.summary: Honey graham crackers from whole-wheat flour, brown sugar, a spoonful of molasses and cinnamon.

ingredients.prep: mixed with ¼ teaspoon cinnamon, for the tops

equipment: food processor or bowl and pastry cutter
steps: Pulse the flours, brown sugar, baking soda, baking powder, salt and cinnamon in the food processor. Add the butter and pulse until it looks like coarse crumbs.
Stir the honey, molasses, milk and vanilla together, pour in, and pulse just until the dough clumps. Press it into two flat squares, wrap, and chill 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 350°F. Roll each square between two sheets of parchment to about ⅛ inch thick, a rough 10 × 12-inch rectangle. Peel off the top sheet.

Trim the edges, cut into 2½ × 5-inch rectangles, and score each across the middle. Prick them with a fork in rows, and sprinkle with cinnamon sugar if you like. Slide the parchment onto a baking sheet; the crackers can touch.
Bake 14 to 18 minutes, until browned at the edges and firm in the middle. Cool on the pan; they crisp as they cool. Re-cut along the lines while still warm.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the container on the counter, about 30 minutes.

keeps: Pantry: airtight once completely cool, 2 to 3 weeks (NDSU’s time for homemade cookies).
Freezer: the wrapped dough or the baked crackers, about 3 months.
scratch.scaling: Roll evenly: thin spots burn and thick ones stay soft. Scraps can be re-rolled once.
scratch.old_way: Sylvester Graham, a minister and diet reformer of the 1830s, urged people to eat bread made from coarse, unsifted whole-wheat flour, which came to be called graham flour. The sweet graham crackers sold today came later and are quite different from the plain ones his followers ate.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: Graham flour is coarsely ground whole-wheat flour; regular whole-wheat flour works nearly the same.
For s’mores, bake them a little thinner and crisper so they snap cleanly.
